meta.title: NYC’s Urban Textscape
meta.description: Reading All of the Words Found on NYC’s Streets
meta.byline: Data by Yufeng Zhao. Story by Matt Daniels

slides.text: What if you could search every visible word on New York City’s streets?
First, we’d need to transcribe every business sign, bumper sticker, ads, flyers—anything with text.
And all these transcribed words are a wealth of information: non-english text could indicate a cultural enclave, like this one in Sunset Park, Brooklyn.
We can pinpoint the phrases that comprise NYC vernacular.
Including the ones that uniquely blanket the city.
If you know, you know.
The possibilities are endless.

section.value: In fact, this is possible because media artist Yufeng Zhou fed millions panoramas from Google Streetview into a computer program, transcribing any text in the images.

The result is a search engine of much of what’s written in NYC’s streets, but limited to text that a Google Streetview car can capture; we’re, of course, missing text from places such as alleyways and parks, or anything too small to be viewable by the camera.
The scale of the data is immense: over 8 million Google Streetview images (from the past 18 years) and 138 million identified snippets of text.
Just to get a sense of scale for the data, we looked at the geography of “pizza,” which unsurprisingly blankets the city. Some words, however, have a clear pattern.

slides.text: Mapping instances of Broadway produces a very obvious map of Broadway. But it’s also beautiful, depicting each borough’s Broadway (all 5 boroughs have one!). View “Broadway” Images
slides.title: Broadway

slides.text: Zooming into Times Square, “Broadway” expands to depict Broadway theaters.
Every new residential building calls itself “luxury,” but only Hudson Yards has applied the label to an entire neighborhood. View “Luxury” Images
slides.title: Luxury

slides.text: There's a simple answer to why “beware” has such a clear geographic footprint, oddly completely absent from Manhattan. At the end of this article, we’ll show you why that is!
slides.title: Beware

slides.text: The map of “gold” depicts Manhattan’s Diamond District, as well as streets lined with “we buy gold” jewelry and pawn shops.
slides.title: Gold

slides.text: Some of the more interesting maps depict cultural enclaves. Coordinates for “iglesia” (church, in Spanish) indicate Spanish-speaking communities.
slides.title: Iglesia

slides.text: Similarly, jerk (the cooking style, not the personality) points to Jamaican enclaves in Flatbush, Brooklyn and Jamaica (the neighborhood) in Queens.
slides.title: Jerk

section.value: The actually Streetview imagery are also revealing. With a simple search, we can see how these words appear on NYC streets.

slides.text: First, here’s probably the most Brooklyn phrase ever, which actually appears on signs as you exit the borough.
slides.title: Fuhgeddaboudit

slides.text: We were able to capture most graffiti text (and tags!)—anything visible from the street.
slides.title: Acab

slides.text: Some text was temporary and indefinitely memorialized in Google Streetview images.
slides.title: Covid

section.value: Most of the data is uninteresting. “Stop” is the #1 word in the dataset, appearing 1,304,417 times, followed by “One way.” No surprises there. But a few phrases are background noise to most people, and once you see it, you can’t unsee it.

slides.text: First, here are the most common words and phrases in our data.
As expected, many of these are related to driving, traffic, and street signs, words that you’d find on any streetscape in the US.
Let’s filter these out, so we can explore the more surprising terms that appear in NYC.
Fedders, at #28, is the logo of an A/C brand that had their units built into the exterior of buildings, from the 1950s to the 1990s, as through-the-wall slots.
slides.post: The logo is so common it’s so common that houses adorned with the phrase have earned the name “Fedders houses,” a pejorative for “reviled” post-WW2 construction. Since they don’t make A/C units for this integrated design anymore, so the ubiquitous Fedders logo is the result of people leaving the decade-old Fedders-branded metal cover on the obsolete A/C slot.

slides.text: At #122 is Yodock, a brand of orange and white plastic barriers, often seen in make-shift sidewalks around construction areas.
Acars is actually “4cars,” misread by our algorithm for translating text in images. The Cash4Cars signs are (illegally) affixed to street signs and lamp posts throughout the city.
slides.post: Apparently in 2021, the Staten Island District Attorney arrested at least one of the men behind the operation on issued 62 summonses.

slides.text: Nathan’s might have the hot dog brand cachet, but Sabrett has the territory, with carts in most NYC tourist traps.
slides.post: Apparently you can rent a Sabrett cart for your next event!

slides.text: NYC has the largest Muslim populations in the US, so it’s no surprise that halal comes in at #351.
slides.post: Halal carts started in the 1980s and are now a staple NYC street food, so much so that NYC mayoral Democratic party nominee Zohran Mamdani campaigned on this relatability with his “halalflation” promise: to lower the cost of chicken over rice by $2.

slides.text: Siamese refers to a type of hose connection for firefighters. More modern (and less racially-charged) names include FDC (Fire Department Connection) and standpipe connection.
Earlier, we depicted the geography of beware, which is concentrated in residential areas fortunate enough to have lawns and fencing. Here we see how popular the phrase is, ranking in the top 1,000.
In case you didn’t already know, you're being surveilled all over NYC. The NYPD, businesses, developers, and even the Parks Department are more than happy to remind you they're recording.
